beats.say: Cover one row of this toucan's bill. Hand the painter just the total, ten pixels. Counting from zero, where should the orange run start?

Ten tells us how wide to make the canvas. It leaves the boundaries between colors open. Here is the missing information. In order, the runs are three yellow, one cream, four orange, and two for the dark tip.

A GPU lane is a thread's position inside a warp. Give one run to each lane. A reduction returns one value from many inputs. A scan returns one value for each position. Keep the run lengths. We will use a scan to put that missing row back.

title: How many inputs does each sum own?

beats.say: Start with the eight lane values on screen. Imagine eight strips of pixels from the same image. Pair the neighboring strips. How wide is each pair?
The first pair adds four and one to make five. The other pairs work at the same time. Each sum spans exactly the two strips that supplied it. Which four strips belong to the next sum on the left?

Combine neighboring partials again. Five and nine make fourteen on the left. Eight and fourteen make twenty-two on the right. One final addition produces thirty-six. Follow any original strip and it reaches the root exactly once.

Count the joins. Four, then two, then one makes seven additions. A balanced tree needs three communication stages for eight leaves. A sequential sum uses seven additions along one chain. The tree shortens the longest dependency while doing the same arithmetic.

title: Can an empty lane send zero?

beats.say: Inside a CUDA warp, thirty-two lanes can exchange register values with a shuffle. Here twenty-six lanes hold one pixel each. Six more stay alive with zero in their registers. At offset sixteen, lane ten asks lane twenty-six for a value. What comes back?
It receives zero. The source lane participated and held zero. Keep the same full mask. Replay the read after lane twenty-six exits. What can lane ten add this time, and why?

The read is undefined. A mask names the participating lanes. It cannot supply a missing register. Every named lane that has not exited must execute the matching shuffle with the same mask. Restore the live zero before continuing.

Run the down-shuffles at offsets sixteen, eight, four, two and one. At each step a lane adds only when its source index is inside the warp. Everyone executes the shuffle before that guard. Lane zero finishes with twenty-six. These exchanges use registers, so they incur no shared-memory bank conflicts. Shared-memory writes still need their own ordering.

title: When may the reader use both slots?

beats.say: Give two warps in one block four real inputs each. Their other lanes carry zero. Each leader owns one partial, fourteen or twenty-two. The first leader writes fourteen into shared memory. The second is still holding twenty-two. Can another warp add both slots yet?

The second leader must write its slot. Then every thread in this block reaches the same block barrier. Put the barrier outside the leaders' branch. After it releases, the reader can load both partials and combine them. Fourteen plus twenty-two gives thirty-six.

In a full block of two hundred fifty-six threads, eight warp leaders each write a shared slot. After the barrier, warp zero loads all eight and fills its other twenty-four registers with zero. It reduces again. Its lane zero owns the block result.

Across blocks, give every block its own global slot. In the lab, a thread checks two input addresses, two hundred fifty-six elements apart. A block can cover five hundred twelve inputs. With just over four million inputs, how many partials will the next pass have to read?

The first pass writes eight thousand one hundred ninety-two partials. A later kernel in the same stream reduces those to sixteen, then another reduces sixteen to one. Widen the input before the first addition so the partials use signed sixty-four-bit arithmetic.

Suppose four blocks occupy all four resident slots. If each waits for four queued blocks, those four may never start. An ordinary block barrier covers one block. A grid barrier requires a supported cooperative launch sized for co-residency.

Another choice is atomic accumulation. Each block adds its partial to one initialized global sum. That saves a separate combine pass but concentrates updates at one address. Use an atomic operation that supports your signed type. Compare the cost of that contention with the cost of extra launches and partial buffers.
Return to the bill. Each lane holds its run length. Freeze this row so every lane can read the same old counts. If orange reaches left by one lane, which two runs does it have?

Cream joins orange. One plus four gives five. The three eligible lanes make their additions together. The new row reads three, four, five, six. Look at the last lane. Six covers orange and the dark tip. Where is the missing first part?

Reach back two places in that saved row. The four at lane one joins six at the tip and gives ten. Three joins five at orange and gives eight. Two rounds of Hillis-Steele give the inclusive prefixes. Each edge counts through its own run. Find the edge after cream. Where can orange begin?

At pixel four. Yellow starts at zero and each later run starts at the previous run's end. Those starts are the exclusive prefixes. Let all four lanes paint their own intervals. Orange covers pixels four through seven, then the dark tip takes eight and nine.

title: How does a tree distribute starts?

beats.say: The pixel lengths were positive. Prefixes can fall as well. Take four signed plays, three, minus one, four, one. In a Blelloch scan, the up-sweep saves two in the left pair and five in the right. Their total is seven. Save it, then replace the root with zero. What score does the right pair start with?

Two. The left subtree inherits the parent's zero. The right subtree inherits zero plus the old left sum. Repeat the split at the leaves. The starting scores are zero, three, two, six. Add each play to its own starting score for the inclusive row. A shared-memory implementation orders each phase before the next reads it.

Count work on thirty-two inputs. Hillis-Steele uses five rounds and one hundred twenty-nine additions. Blelloch walks up and back down, using ten rounds and sixty-two additions. At five hundred twelve inputs the work gap grows to about fourfold. Addition counts alone cannot tell you the faster kernel. Time the memory traffic and barriers too.

title: Where must the second trace begin?

beats.say: Split the eight plays after the first four. Each block has drawn its score trace from zero. The first block ends at seven. The second block's local score before its nine-point penalty is five. Where should the second trace start on the global scoreboard?

Lift the entire right trace by seven. The score before the penalty becomes twelve. After the penalty it falls to three. An exclusive scan of the block totals, seven and four, supplies offsets zero and seven. Add a block's offset to every local prefix. A clean memory check can still miss a missing offset.

The block totals may need a scan of their own. A width of five hundred twelve fits five hundred twelve totals in one tile. Add one more input to a full square of tiles. The resulting five hundred thirteen totals need two metadata tiles, then one.

A single-pass alternative is decoupled look-back. Our tile holds two. Going left, it finds a published aggregate of three, another of four, then a completed prefix of seven. Stop there. Its starting offset is fourteen. Its ending prefix is sixteen. Publish that prefix so the next tile can use it. This tile can write corrected outputs directly.

What if that first record is still empty? Wait for the payload. The producer writes the value before release-publishing its status. The reader acquires that status before using the value. A scheduler must also let predecessors run. A bare flag cannot guarantee either property.

Give two addition trees the same three Float32 inputs. One hundred million, its negative, and about three point one four. Pair the large values first and they cancel. Add the residual next. It survives. Keep that answer while the other tree runs.

In the second tree, add the residual to the large negative value first. At this scale neighboring floats are eight apart. Follow the exact sum to its nearest representable value. Which intermediate will the register keep?
It rounds back to minus one hundred million. Pause with that rounded value still in the register. Now add positive one hundred million. What is left?

Zero. Both trees were race-free. A fixed tree can repeat an inaccurate answer. With the residual as reference and absolute tolerance point zero two, the zero misses by about three point one four. Check distance from the reference separately from bitwise repeatability across runs. Compare two runs of a different kernel against the same reference. Suppose it gives three point one three, then three point one five. The bits changed. Both results are within tolerance.

Integer partials have a different limit. Pair the largest signed sixty-four-bit integer with one, then subtract one. The final mathematical sum fits. The first pair overflows. Check the range of every intermediate or widen it before adding.

title: What changes when a larger logit arrives?

beats.say: Before turning scores into probabilities, collect their exponential mass. For finite logits two and one, subtract the largest, two. The contributions are one and e to the minus one. The first chunk's denominator is about one point three six eight.

The next chunk contains four and zero. Its maximum is four and its mass at that scale is about one point zero one eight. Both chunks have good sums, but they use different reference points. What happens to the first chunk when we measure it from four?

Rescale the earlier sum by e to the minus two. Its contribution at four is about point one eight five. The new chunk already uses four. Add the two masses on that common scale. The merged denominator is about one point two zero three, including the full unit from the largest logit.

The state carries both the maximum and a rescaled sum. To merge two nonempty chunks, choose the larger maximum. Multiply each sum by the exponential of its old maximum minus that common maximum. Then add. An empty chunk contributes zero mass and can be skipped before subtracting maxima.
Four logit reads gave us the maximum and denominator. Imagine those two numbers are all we kept on chip. Four probability slots are still empty. Which inputs must we read to fill them?

Read each logit again. For every slot, exponentiate its logit minus four, then divide by the final denominator. The first result is about eleven percent. Four more reads fill all four slots. Keeping the logits on chip could avoid a trip back to memory. Subtracting a finite maximum bounds the exponentials by one. Tiny contributions can still underflow.

An attention kernel can ask for a weighted vector. For logits two and one in chunk A, each value points one unit right. For logits four and zero in chunk B, each value points one unit up. When the maximum rises, rescale the old weighted sum and the old denominator together. Add the new values on that scale and divide by the total mass. The result points mostly up.

That on-chip accumulator lets tiled attention emit the weighted result without storing the full score matrix. At fixed head width, output storage grows linearly with sequence length. Pairwise attention arithmetic still grows quadratically. Masked logits contribute zero. This model rejects other nonfinite logits and a fully masked row.

Keep just the positive plays in order. Turn the signed inputs into flags, one for keep and zero for skip. Scan the flags exclusively. Minus one and four both see one earlier positive, so they have the same destination. Which one writes there?

Only four writes there. A zero flag suppresses the write. The retained values fill a separate output buffer in input order. An inclusive flag scan would count the item itself and shift the destinations.

Now ask for one sum per segment. Split the eight plays at four, then at four again. The repeated boundary makes the middle range empty. Keep its output slot. The sums are seven, zero and four. Zero is the identity for addition.

To find a winner, reduce value and source index together. On this short replay two sixes tie. Our rule keeps the smaller index. The winning pair is six at index zero. This rule assumes a nonempty row of finite values.

title: What would a fair timing include?

beats.say: A library scan can give a separate packing kernel its addresses. A fused kernel can use an address while it is still in a register. For the four-point play going to slot one, which memory traffic disappears?

The address write and its later read disappear. Compare the full fused path with DeviceScan plus the same packing operation. Match data types, output order, determinism and setup boundaries. Use DeviceReduce for a whole-array total. Inside a kernel, BlockScan and BlockReduce cooperate on one tile.

In the CUDA lab, allocate and upload before timing. Reuse scratch after its stream finishes. Warm up five times, then time thirty complete operations with events. Include recursive passes and the final scalar copy for reduction. The saved receipt used an older build. Measure the current source on your GPU.

For a scan of one thousand twenty-four items, count four bytes read and eight written per item. At three microseconds that gives about four point one decimal gigabytes per second of useful data. Extra metadata and cache hits change physical traffic. This calculation gives a logical byte rate.

Before timing, compare every output against a serial reference. Exercise warp, tile and recursion boundaries. Use memcheck for address errors, racecheck for conflicting shared-memory accesses, and synccheck for barrier misuse. A lucky schedule can hide a missing barrier. A clean executed run leaves other schedules open.

Try a fresh row of five run lengths in two four-lane tiles. Only the first five lanes own real runs. The other three carry zero through the tile collective and skip global loads and stores. What address does the last real run need?
Ten. Its local exclusive prefix is zero. The first tile contributes ten, so the last owner starts at ten and paints five pixels. The complete row is fifteen pixels wide.
Swap just the one-pixel and five-pixel runs across the tile boundary. The total width is still fifteen. Before the last run paints, what starting address should its owner get this time?

Fourteen. The first tile now contributes fourteen and the last tile contributes one. A reduction would pass the same total check on both rows. An exclusive scan gives each owner the right starting pixel. Compare every address, including the last real one, with the serial trace.
